title: Tell Me What Youre Excited About
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Citing Virginia Woolf's line that 'pleasure has no relish unless we share it,' this Field Note explores why people are reluctant to share genuine excitement, even though research shows sharing positive experiences boosts well-being and life satisfaction. Reasons for hesitancy include fear of rejection, worry about seeming unprofessional, and concern about others' envy. The recommended fix is proactive: good leaders explicitly ask team members what excites them, creating a safe, protective space where enthusiasm is welcomed rather than risking that people keep it to themselves.
points: Research links sharing positive experiences and excitement with heightened well-being and life satisfaction.
People often withhold excitement due to fear of rejection, appearing unprofessional, or others' envy.
Leaders are encouraged to proactively ask team members what they're excited about rather than waiting for it to surface.
Creating a supportive, protective atmosphere is framed as essential to normalizing shared enthusiasm.
Virginia Woolf's observation that pleasure requires sharing anchors the piece's argument about workplace excitement.
quotes: Research confirms that discussing positive experiences with others leads to heightened well-being, more energy, and increased life satisfaction.
The hesitancy to share excitement can spring from several sources. One fear is the possible rejection or criticism of a new idea.
Good leaders recognize the importance of sharing excitement with others and the reluctance of many team members to do so.
The famed writer Virginia Woolf had it right when she wrote, “Pleasure has no relish unless we share it.
Good leaders always add relish to everyone’s excitement. They constantly ask others to share their excitement to the benefit of everyone.
